I am reading Airey Neave's NUREMBERG – A PERSONAL RECORD OF THE TRIAL OF THE MAJOR NAZI WAR CRIMINALS.

I had read the book years ago when it was published in paperback and I am now rereading bits and pieces before giving most of my books away.

I open the book at random. It opens at the chapter headed A COMPETENT OFFICER. The chapter describes Neave handing the indictment to Alfried Jodl.

… The cell door was flung open and showed him standing in an old tunic with grey breeches and felt slippers instead of his shining black boots. He stood quietly to attention as if waiting to receive instructions. There was an impatient pause around me, then I spoke.

'Alfried Yodl?'

'Yes.'

I noticed that he was looking sharply at my Sam Browne. He displayed no emotion. When I had explained my mission to him he began to speak in a brisk, polite manner. I could visualise him at Hitler's conferences, lucid, courteous and relentless for he had been Chief of the Operations Staff of Hitler's armed forces.

'Will you advise me, Herr Major, what sort of lawyer I should have to defend me?'

'What do you mean?'

I was nonplussed. Jodl continued incisively as if he were addressing an ill-informed junior officer.

'I wish to know whether it would be best to have as my advocate a lawyer who is an expert in international law or one who is an experienced in criminal law.'

This was a difficult question. The indictment involved questions of both criminal and international law.

I replied, 'The indictment charges you with with war crimes and crimes against humanity. I can ascertain for you the qualifications of the people on this list of German lawyers.'

It was not an entirely satisfactory answer and I had to consult the tribunal before returning next day to discuss suitable lawyers with Jodl and some of the other defendants.

Jodl was a cool customer. He stood there with the indictment, his hands quite steady as he fingered it. He turned to me again obviously contemptuous of my previous answer.

'I shall read this document and consider the point. I am already preparing my defence. You will understand how difficult it is without paper and pencils. Can you help me to get some?'

I felt half-amused sympathy for the brilliant general staff officer deprived of paper and pencil. There was no self-pity about him, certainly no tears. Thus had he perfected Hitler's military plans to dominate Europe by force of arms. It must have been in the same calm fashion that he had agreed to the shooting of unarmed prisoners of war.
